newsitem.title: USA: US CORPORATE BONDS-LILCO bonds spike on LIPA news.
newsitem.headline: US CORPORATE BONDS-LILCO bonds spike on LIPA news.

text.p: A large financial transaction by the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA) electrified the bonds of the Long Island Lighting Co (LILCO) in the U.S. corporate bond market on Tuesday, traders said.
Investment-grade bonds were otherwise firm but unchanged on Tuesday, while junk bond prices rose 1/4 of a point, continuing to gain strength from the solid new issue market, traders said.
On Tuesday afternoon, word spread that LIPA had set up a $4.5 billion interest rate swap in connection with its planned partial takeover of LILCO.
LIPA plans to sell nearly $7.3 billion in municipal debt to finance the acquisition of certain LILCO assets. Under the plan, the remaining businesses of LILCO will merged with Brooklyn Union Gas.
LILCO outstanding bonds tightened five to 15 basis points as news of the LIPA swap leaked to the market, traders said.

"This was seen as a vote of confidence in the transaction and the prospects for the deal being consummated. It makes sense the bonds would tighten," said John Spellman, utilities debt analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. Traders noted LILCO's debentures outperformed the utility's other outstanding bonds as investors speculated that they were more likely to be assumed by LIPA under the transaction.
"The debentures are where you want to be," said one trader. "There is a decent shot that the (new LIPA) will tender them and refinance them with lower cost municipal debt," he added.
In other news, Grand Union Co bonds stabilized on Tuesday after plummeting approximately 20 points over the past week.
The company's bonds were quoted 45-46 by one trader.
Traders are now waiting for the supermarket company to hire a replacement for Joseph McCaig, its chief executive officer who resigned in May.
"This was supposed to be July's business," said one trader. "Fear of a delay is one of the reasons people have been taking out the bonds and shooting them."
The bonds have also been battered by market concerns the company may be unable to make an upcoming interest payment.
In the primary market, Marsh Supermarkets Inc sold $150 million of 10-year senior notes in a 144a private placement via Merrill Lynch & Co on Tuesday.
The company, which operates supermakets in Ohio and Indiana, priced the B2/B-plus-rated bonds to yield 9 percent.

Among investment-grade issuers, Merrill Lynch & Co sold $500 million in seven-year debt, ConAgra Inc sold $300 million in 30-year bonds, puttable in 12 years, and Quebecor Printing Inc, a unit of Quebecor Inc sold $150 million in 30-year bonds.
In other markets, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 53.42 points to end the day at 8174.53.
A technical rally in U.S. Treasuries late on Tuesday, helped the market overcame early losses which resulted from employment cost index data.

On Tuesday morning, the Labor Deparment reported that the employment cost index rose 0.8 percent in the second quarter. Although the number was as expected, the market had hoped for a weaker than consensus figure like the prior few reports.
The price of the benchmark 30-year Treasury ended the day 7/32 higher at 103-4/32. Its yield fell to 6.39 percent.
((--Douglas Brown, U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1662))
